newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's Defence Council readies army reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's Defence Council readies army reforms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin chairs a key meeting of the Kremlin Defence Council on Thursday to consider the fate of Russia's armed forces, reeling from a barrage of corruption charges against the top brass.

The meeting comes after military prosecutors on Wednesday arrested one of the country's top generals, deputy defence minister Konstantin Kobets, previously acclaimed as a hero for his defence of Yeltsin in the failed 1991 hardline communist coup.
It was the latest drama in a high-profile anti-graft drive that has left vacancies in some top jobs whose new occupants will guide army reforms into the next century.

With the government mired in a profound budget crisis and Yeltsin flying to Paris next week to sign a treaty with Moscow's Cold War adversary NATO, much-delayed modernisation and slimming down of the bloated armed forces is more pressing than ever.

Yeltsin promised during his re-election campaign a year ago to end conscription by the year 2000 and create a modern, professional army. With conscripts dying in their thousands in the debacle of his Chechen campaign, that was good politics.

Since then, the realities of funding expensive reforms and a marked lack of enthusiasm in the upper ranks have seen the deadline quietly shelved. Yeltsin was seriously ill for the first eight months of his new term, further hampering progress.
Now, however, the 66-year-old president, conscious of having just three years left to write himself into history as a successful ruler, has recovered some of his zeal for change.

After shaking up the government by promoting a team of young economic liberals, he seems ready to take on the military, whose 1.8 million men under arms and privileged heritage as a pillar of the Soviet system make it a key component of Russian society.

Yeltsin's anti-corruption campaign is being spearheaded by government economy chiefs like First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, who see it as vital to restoring the state finances and winning public confidence.
The biggest heads to roll so far have been in the military, creating vacancies that, as with the cabinet, will give Yeltsin the chance to promote reformers.
Interfax news agency said on Wednesday the Defence Council may name a successor to Land Forces Commander General Vladimir Semyonov, who was sacked after corruption charges last month.
The likely candidate, the agency said, is General Viktor Chechevatov, commander of the Far East military district, who is close to the Kremlin leader. Other top posts may also be filled.

On his arrest on Wednesday, an ailing General Kobets was taken from hospital where he was being treated and whisked away for questioning at Moscow's notorious Lefortovo prison. Military prosecutors said he faced corruption charges.

Military prosecutors say as many as 20 generals and 100 colonels are under investigation for graft. Stories abound of army stores, from rations to rockets, being sold off for private profit and of defence contractors building lavish country dachas for the top brass in exchange for lucrative army orders.
The situation is all the more scandalous because the vast majority of officers and men live on the bread line.
The longer term strategy for military reform is muddied by differences between the military and civilian planners, notably Defence Council secretary Yuri Baturin, a trusted Yeltsin aide.
Many top generals have been reluctant to scale back a force designed to withstand a massed onslaught from the West.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who hung up his uniform in December to become Russia's first civilian in the post, warns that reforms will be very expensive.

But the bloodletting in the upper ranks, a new security doctrine which plays down the risk of all-out attack from abroad and a treaty with NATO to be signed next week, all point to the balance swinging in favour of a smaller, more flexible army.
